work.label: Selected engineering work
work.title: Four products, explained from the inside
work.intro: The applications I can talk about at the greatest depth. Each one covers what it does, how it is put together, what it talks to, and exactly which part of it is mine. MentorX and Hen Lehen are platforms: two separate applications each, sharing one backend.

cases.name: Flowrist
cases.summary: A flower-delivery app: browse a catalog, manage a cart, check out and pay, then track the order on a map. The Flutter client talks to a .NET microservice platform — identity, catalog, cart, orders, payments and addresses — behind one API gateway.
highlights: Twenty-five typed endpoints across six services, reached through Retrofit clients organised by feature rather than one shared API object.
A token layer built as four collaborating pieces — storage, refresher, scheduler and a coordinator that makes concurrent 401s wait on a single refresh instead of each firing their own.
Device sessions as a real feature: the app lists its own active sessions, registers its FCM token against the identity service, and can sign a device out.
cases.backend: A .NET microservice platform, not a single server: identity, catalog, address-cart, orders and payments are separate services behind one API gateway, with SQL Server, RabbitMQ for messaging and Redis. The Flutter app addresses them through gateway-prefixed routes — /api/identity, /api/catalog, /api/address-cart — using Retrofit clients. Payments go through Stripe, push notifications through Firebase Cloud Messaging, and the repository carries a Docker Compose file that brings the whole backend up locally.
cases.role: Team project. Her README records that she worked as a Flutter/mobile developer on the team that built the app, contributing to the mobile client inside the shared Clean Architecture structure, and that the repository is maintained independently under her own account with the original team's permission.

architecture.intro: Feature-first Clean Architecture: nine features — auth, commerce, cart, address, order, payment, profile, notification and sessions — each owning its own api, data, domain and presentation folders, with everything shared living in core. Dependency injection is generated rather than hand-wired: injectable annotations appear across 115 files. The same shape is used for every feature, so a new one is a folder rather than a decision.

BLoC and Cubit view-models per feature
go_router for routing, including the payment return

flow.title: Placing an order
steps: The catalog loads page by page through infinite_scroll_pagination, with cached images and a shimmer placeholder while a page resolves.
Details are fetched by id from the catalog service.
Items are added, quantities patched and items removed against the address-cart service.
A delivery address is picked on the map and reverse-geocoded into a stored address.
Payment goes through Stripe; the app returns to a route go_router keeps for it.
The order is placed, then tracked on a map with the route drawn from OSRM.

decisions: Give each feature its own Retrofit client instead of one shared API object, so six services behind a gateway stay six readable surfaces.
Split the token layer into storage, refresher, scheduler and coordinator, because a single refresh function could not express "everyone waits for one refresh".
Register the routing Dio instance under its own name, so a third-party routing outage can never be reported as an authentication failure.
Read the gateway URL and the map key from .env, so nothing environment-specific is committed.

challenges.title: Several requests meeting an expired token at once
challenges.problem: When a token expires, every in-flight request fails with 401 at roughly the same moment. The naive fix — refresh inside the error interceptor — makes each failed request start its own refresh, and the server invalidates all but one of them.
challenges.constraint: The refresh had to happen once, the waiting requests had to be replayed with the new token, and the user had to notice nothing.
challenges.approach: Separate the concerns: storage holds the tokens, a refresher performs the exchange, a scheduler refreshes ahead of expiry, and a coordinator serialises everything so concurrent callers await one in-flight refresh.
challenges.implementation: core/network/: token_storage.dart, token_refresher.dart, token_refresh_scheduler.dart and token_refresh_coordinator.dart, with auth_interceptors.dart as the only place that reacts to a 401.
challenges.outcome: Concurrent 401s now resolve through one refresh and the waiting requests are replayed, instead of racing and invalidating each other.

challenges.title: Six services behind one gateway
challenges.problem: The backend is not one API. Identity, catalog, address-cart, orders and payments are separate services, each with its own route prefix, and a single shared API client would have become a dumping ground.
challenges.constraint: Routes had to stay readable and typed, and a feature should not have to know about services it does not use.
challenges.approach: One Retrofit client per feature, with all paths declared as named constants in one endpoints file so the gateway prefixes are visible in a single place.
challenges.implementation: core/constants endpoint constants, with clients such as features/sessions/api/session_api_client.dart and the matching clients under each feature.
challenges.outcome: Adding a service means adding a client beside its feature; no shared API object grows every time the backend does.

challenges.title: A map that has to answer three different questions
challenges.problem: The same map is used to pick a delivery address, to show where an order is, and to draw the route to it — three jobs with different data and different failure modes.
challenges.constraint: Location permission can be refused, geocoding can fail, and routing is a third-party service that may not answer.
challenges.approach: Keep the map a dumb renderer and put each job behind its own repository: reverse geocoding goes to the address service, routing to OSRM through a separate Dio instance registered under its own name.
challenges.implementation: A named osrmDio registration keeps routing calls off the authenticated client, so a routing failure can never look like an auth failure.
challenges.outcome: A routing failure shows as a routing problem, and the user stays signed in.

quality.summary: The test suite is the strongest in the portfolio: 130 test files containing roughly 636 test cases, organised to mirror lib/ — per feature, per layer, with fixtures and helpers of their own. Tests use mockito for generated doubles and bloc_test for view-model behaviour. A GitHub Actions workflow checks pull-request titles, and the Flutter version is pinned with FVM.
items: 130 test files, ~636 cases, mirroring the lib/ structure
mockito for generated mocks, bloc_test for view-models
Fixtures and shared test helpers rather than inline setup
CI workflow on pull requests; Flutter version pinned via .fvmrc
Runtime configuration through .env rather than committed constants

limits: The backend services are the team's work; this repository holds the Flutter client plus the Docker Compose file that runs them.
Running the app needs a .env with the gateway base URL and a MapTiler key; neither is committed.

cases.name: Tracking App
cases.summary: A delivery-driver client for a last-mile product: a driver applies with licence and vehicle documents, signs in, and their live position and route to pickup and customer are tracked on a map.
highlights: A driver application that uploads licence and national-ID images as a multipart request alongside vehicle type, plate and capacity.
A forgot-password flow modelled as a three-step state machine — email, one-time code, new password — with resend handled without losing the step.
Live location reported to the server, with permission and location-service checks gating the map, and the route drawn from an open routing service.
cases.backend: A REST backend reached through Retrofit clients split by concern — identity and orders. Nine endpoints are wired: sign in, driver application as a multipart upload, vehicle types, forgot password, verify OTP, reset password and driver location reporting. An interceptor refreshes the bearer token on a 401 and retries the request once. The base URL is read from an environment file rather than committed. Route geometry comes from the public OSRM routing service, which is a third-party API rather than part of the backend.
cases.role: Team project. Her README records that she worked as a Flutter/mobile developer on the team that built it, and that the application is now maintained independently under her own account with the original team's permission.

flow.title: From application to delivery
steps: Licence and national-ID images go up with vehicle type, plate and capacity as one multipart request.
A bearer token is issued and stored in secure storage.
Location permission and the location service are both checked before the map is shown.
The live position is reported to the server while the driver works.
The route to pickup and customer is drawn from an open routing service.

decisions: Split identity and orders into separate Retrofit clients, so a change to sign-in cannot ripple into delivery calls.
Model forgot-password as a three-step state machine rather than three screens, so a resend cannot lose the step.
Keep the base URL in an environment file so the repository carries no environment-specific host.

challenges.title: A driver signed out mid-delivery
challenges.problem: An expired token during a delivery would drop the driver back to the login screen, losing the route and the job in progress.
challenges.constraint: The refresh had to be invisible, and a genuinely invalid session still had to end cleanly.
challenges.approach: Handle 401 inside an interceptor: refresh the bearer token, replay the original request exactly once, and only surface an error if the replay also fails.
challenges.implementation: core/network/: auth_interceptors.dart with token_refresh.dart and token_storage.dart beside it.
challenges.outcome: An expired token is refreshed and the request replayed, so a driver mid-delivery is not returned to the login screen.

challenges.title: Uploading documents and data in one request
challenges.problem: The driver application sends licence and national-ID images together with vehicle type, plate and capacity — a mixed payload that is easy to get wrong field by field.
challenges.constraint: It had to stay typed and testable rather than a hand-built form map.
challenges.approach: Declare it as a typed Retrofit multipart endpoint so the client generates the body, and keep the images as part of the same request rather than a second upload step.
challenges.implementation: A @MultiPart() @POST(ApiEndpoints.applyDriver) definition on the identity client.
challenges.outcome: The documents and the vehicle data arrive together, so there is no half-finished application on the server.

challenges.title: A map that must not lie
challenges.problem: Location permission can be refused, the location service can be off, and the routing service is third-party — any of which would otherwise show an empty or wrong map.
challenges.constraint: The driver needs to know which of those happened, not just see a blank screen.
challenges.approach: Gate the map behind explicit permission and service checks, and keep route geometry in its own repository so a routing outage is reported as a routing problem.
challenges.implementation: geolocator for permission and position, flutter_map for rendering, and an OSRM route endpoint declared separately from the app's own API.
challenges.outcome: A permission refusal or a routing outage is reported as itself, instead of showing an empty map.

quality.summary: 26 test files covering the blocs, the use cases and the data mappers. The networking split pays off here: identity can be tested without standing up order fixtures.
items: 26 test files across features and core
freezed DTOs, so a missing field is a compile error rather than a null at runtime
Base URL and secrets read from an environment file, never committed
Feature branches with reviewed merges on the original team repository

limits: The backend is the team's, not in this repository.
Route geometry depends on a public OSRM instance, which is fine for a prototype and would need a hosted router in production.

cases.name: MentorX
cases.summary: A learning platform for school students and their parents, built as a Flutter monorepo of around seventy packages. Two separate applications sit on one shared platform layer and one REST API.
highlights: One package per repository, each with a Dio implementation and a mock twin behind the same interface, so a feature can be written and tested before the endpoint exists.
A single HTTP client carries the token, device id and locale, and refreshes an expired token in an interceptor before replaying the call — both applications authenticate identically.
Arabic and English localisation lives in the shared UI package: around nine hundred lines of strings regenerated through the project's code-generation step, which both apps pick up.
cases.sharedBackend: The EduCore REST API, the platform's own backend, reached through twenty Dio repository packages — one per domain: authentication, home, courses, quizzes, assignments, grades, attendance, wallet, marketplace, rewards, leaderboard, announcements, notifications, profile, settings, analytics and more. They all sit on one shared HTTP client whose interceptors attach the token, device id and locale, and refresh an expired token before replaying the call. Each repository has a mock twin, so screens can be built and tested with no server.
cases.myPart: Contributing member of a team led by another developer: 4 of 114 commits. My own work is the localisation layer, the notification-service boundary and its mock, and extensions to the student notification repository and the parent authentication repositories. The learning journeys — courses, quizzes, attendance, wallet, marketplace — are other developers' work.

flow.title: A screen built before its endpoint existed
steps: The domain defines a repository interface in its own package.
A mock package implements it, so the screen can be built and reviewed immediately.
The Dio package implements the same interface once the endpoint lands.
Dependency injection chooses which one is bound; no screen code changes.
The shared client attaches the token, device id and locale, and refreshes before replaying.

decisions: One package per repository, with a mock twin, so work is never blocked by a missing endpoint.
Put the HTTP client in its own package, so both apps authenticate identically instead of duplicating session rules.
Keep every string in the shared UI package and generate typed accessors, so a missing translation fails the build.

challenges.title: Writing features before the endpoints existed
challenges.problem: Screens were being built against an API that was still changing, so work either stalled or was written against a guess.
challenges.constraint: The mock could not be a branch of the real code, or the two would drift.
challenges.approach: Give every domain two packages behind one interface — a Dio implementation and a mock — and let dependency injection decide which is bound.
challenges.implementation: packages/student/dio_*_repository paired with packages/mock/student/mock_*_repository, twenty of each.
challenges.outcome: Features reached review before their endpoints were live, and the swap to real data needed no screen changes.

challenges.title: Two apps, one notion of "signed in"
challenges.problem: The student and parent apps hit the same API with the same token rules, and duplicating the auth plumbing would have meant two places to fix every session bug.
challenges.constraint: They are separate apps and cannot share a runtime.
challenges.approach: Put the HTTP client in its own package with the token, device-id and locale interceptors inside it, and depend on it from both apps.
challenges.implementation: packages/clients/dio_http_client, with header_interceptor.dart and refresh_token_interceptor.dart.
challenges.outcome: Both applications share one definition of a session, so a session bug is fixed once.

challenges.title: Localisation that two apps pick up at once
challenges.problem: Arabic and English strings were needed in both applications and in the shared components, and keeping three copies in step by hand was not realistic.
challenges.constraint: Translations had to be type-safe, so a missing key fails at build time rather than showing a raw identifier to a student.
challenges.approach: Keep every string in the shared UI package and generate typed accessors from it, so both apps consume the same generated source.
challenges.implementation: Slang code generation in packages/mentorx_ui/lib/localization, producing strings.g.dart and strings_ar.g.dart.
challenges.outcome: Arabic and English are picked up by both apps from one generated source.

quality.summary: The mock twins are the quality story here: because every repository has one, a feature can be exercised end to end without a server, and a broken endpoint cannot block a screen from being reviewed.
items: One mock repository per real repository, behind a shared interface
Typed localisation, so a missing translation is a build failure
A notification boundary defined as an interface before any provider was chosen

limits: This is a team product; her contribution is the localisation layer, the notification boundary and the repository extensions named above.
The learning journeys — courses, quizzes, attendance, wallet, marketplace — are other developers' work.
The API host in the committed environment file is a bare IP address, which is fine for development and would need a proper hostname and TLS in production.

cases.name: Hen Lehen
cases.summary: An Arabic-first, women-only telemedicine platform: two separate Flutter applications, one for patients and one for doctors, and a FastAPI backend I built for both.
highlights: The backend is a complete service in its own right: nineteen endpoint modules and sixteen models on PostgreSQL, with Redis, JWT authentication, rate limiting, a WebSocket chat endpoint and seventy-three passing tests.
Both applications are Arabic-first rather than Arabic-added: the layout is wrapped in Directionality and the whole interface runs off a locale provider written by hand, with a light and a dark theme.
Three local packages — shared_core, shared_models and shared_ui — hold the models, theme and components both apps use, so the patient and doctor apps stay consistent without sharing a codebase.
cases.sharedBackend: This is the backend. FastAPI on Python with async SQLAlchemy over PostgreSQL, Redis for caching and rate-limit state, and Alembic migrations. Authentication is JWT issued with python-jose and passwords hashed with passlib/bcrypt; slowapi applies rate limiting, and a WebSocket endpoint carries the consultation chat. Nineteen endpoint modules cover auth, patients, doctors, specialties, appointments, medical records, payments, chat, community, reviews, favourites, branches, notifications, devices, uploads and admin.
cases.myPart: Individually developed: both Flutter applications and the FastAPI backend are mine, 13 commits on the patient app and 18 on the doctor app, plus the backend on its own branch.
cases.gap: The honest gap: the backend is built and tested, and both apps now carry the Dio client, the request interceptor and an authentication repository on their integration branches — but the repository's API call is still commented out, so neither app sends a request yet and both still read an in-memory data set. This is the next piece of work, not a claim about what exists.

flow.title: Booking a consultation (as it runs today)
steps: Filters and sorts the mock doctor list inside the doctors notifier, by specialty and by rating, experience or fee.

decisions: Build the whole journey first, so the product idea could be judged before any backend existed.
Write the locale handling by hand rather than add a code-generation step to a prototype — and record the cost: the keys are duplicated across the two apps.
Audit my own architecture and publish the findings rather than leave the shortcuts undocumented.

challenges.title: An Arabic-first interface, not a translated one
challenges.problem: The product only makes sense in Arabic, so right-to-left could not be an afterthought.
challenges.constraint: No code-generation step, in a prototype that had to stay quick to change.
challenges.approach: A locale provider holding the strings, with the app wrapped in Directionality so direction follows the locale everywhere.
challenges.implementation: config/locale.dart (367 lines) and main.dart:45-50; the chat bubbles in the doctor app were realigned for RTL in a later commit.
challenges.outcome: Both apps run fully in Arabic. The trade-off is real and I wrote it down: the keys are duplicated per app instead of living in one resource.

challenges.title: Reviewing my own codebase honestly
challenges.problem: After the UI was finished, the structure was clearly holding the project back.
challenges.constraint: I was the only developer, so there was no reviewer to find it for me.
challenges.approach: Write the audit as if for someone else: name each problem, locate it, and plan the migration in steps with a risk table.
challenges.implementation: docs/PHASE_1_PROJECT_ANALYSIS.md lists ten issues, including monolithic providers, a theme provider defined three times, duplicated models and no serialisation; docs/PHASE_2_MIGRATION_PLAN.md sets out the migration.
challenges.outcome: The analysis is accurate — I re-checked every finding against the code. The migration itself exists only on side branches, which is why this is shown as a prototype.

quality.summary: There are no tests, and I am not going to present this as more than it is. Static analysis is clean against the pinned shared UI package; against the current one it reports errors, because a change to the shared theme was not carried into the two apps at the same time. The repository's own roadmap lists exactly what is missing — secure tokens, tests, CI, flavours, signing — and leaves every box unchecked.

challenges.title: An approval gate that cannot be walked around
challenges.problem: A doctor whose licence has not been reviewed must not reach the dashboard — and hiding the button is not the same as preventing access.
challenges.constraint: Deep links and back navigation had to respect the gate too.
challenges.approach: Put the rule in the router rather than the UI: until the account is approved, every route redirects to the pending screen, so there is no path to the dashboard at all.
challenges.implementation: A go_router redirect driven by the session provider's approval state.
challenges.outcome: An unapproved account cannot reach the dashboard by deep link or by back navigation.

challenges.title: Right-to-left chat that was quietly wrong
challenges.problem: The chat bubbles were laid out for a left-to-right reading order, so in Arabic the doctor's and the patient's messages sat on the wrong sides of the thread.
challenges.constraint: Mirroring the whole screen would have flipped avatars and timestamps too.
challenges.approach: Align the bubbles to the speaker rather than to the writing direction, and let Directionality handle the text itself.
challenges.implementation: The message row alignment was reworked so the sender determines the side, with the surrounding layout still RTL-aware.

challenges.title: Two apps that must not drift apart

items.name: Elevate Online Exams
items.imageAlt: A timed exam question with four answers and a score card showing 80%.
items.summary: A mobile client for an online-exams platform: students sign in, choose a subject, take timed exams and review their results.
highlights: Session expiry that tells a real expired token from a 401 the API uses for validation, and logs out exactly once when several requests fail together.
A timed exam engine that auto-submits on timeout and asks before the student leaves.
Fixed a crash caused by the API’s history response and merged it with a per-user local history.
items.note: The API, designs and Postman collection were provided by Elevate; the app is my work.

overview.purpose: Let students practise and sit timed exams on their phone.
overview.role: Sole Flutter developer (API and designs provided).

scope.title: Account
items: Sign in with Remember me, sign up with live validation

scope.title: Exams
items: Subjects → exams → start → timed session → score → answer review
Results history with pull-to-refresh that keeps data if a refresh fails

scope.title: Platform
items: Secure token storage and forced logout on session expiry

architecture.intro: Three feature modules (auth, exam, home). Cubits call single-purpose use cases, use cases call repository interfaces, and repositories wrap data sources in a safe-call that returns a sealed result.

flow.title: Submitting an exam
steps: Next on the last question calls cubit.goToNext → submitExam.
Stops the timer, computes time spent, calls SubmitExamUseCase.
Wraps the call in safeCall, which turns exceptions into a Failure.
Maps answers to [{questionId, correct}] and POSTs /questions/check.
Adds the token header; a real 401 clears the session and fires the event bus.
Saves the result per user, newest first, without duplicates.
The listener navigates to the result screen, or shows a SnackBar on failure.

decisions: Networking never touches navigation: session expiry is published on an event bus and handled once at the app root.
Known shortcut: domain interfaces still reference shared data models.

challenges.title: Real session expiry vs. a misused 401
challenges.problem: The API sometimes answers validation errors with 401, and parallel requests can all fail at the same moment.
challenges.constraint: Only a genuinely expired session should log the user out, and only once.
challenges.approach: Classify 401/403 responses by their body, guard against re-entry and decouple networking from navigation.
challenges.implementation: A message heuristic in the interceptor, a re-entrancy flag that resets on sign-in, a SessionEventBus and a second de-duplication guard at the root.
challenges.outcome: Unit tests describe each branch of the rule; one edge case (a 401 with no response) still fails and is next to fix.

challenges.title: A results screen that crashed on real data
challenges.problem: The history endpoint returns null or a single object, not a list, so casting it crashed the tab.
challenges.constraint: The backend contract could not be changed.
challenges.approach: Normalise every shape, parse numbers defensively and keep a local, per-user history.
challenges.implementation: Shape normalisation and enrichment in the data source; local-first merge in the repository so a remote failure is not fatal when local data exists.
challenges.outcome: Fixed in two commits, with model and store tests.

challenges.title: A timed exam that cannot be lost by accident
challenges.problem: Time can run out, and a back gesture can throw away a whole attempt.
challenges.constraint: Async work must not emit after the Cubit is closed.
challenges.approach: Own the timer in the Cubit and make leaving explicit.
challenges.implementation: Timer.periodic cancelled on submit, leave and close; auto-submit on timeout; isClosed checks after every await; PopScope with a leave confirmation.
challenges.outcome: Timeout submits the full duration and leaving needs confirmation.

quality.summary: Unit tests cover the auth interceptor, token service and Remember-me rules, the safe-call wrapper, validators and the local history store, using mocktail and fake_async. As committed, the test dependencies do not resolve on current Flutter; with bloc_test updated, 100 of 109 tests pass, and the failures are a stale smoke test and interceptor-test harness issues still to fix.

items.backend: Elevate's own REST API — a third-party backend provided with the brief, not one of hers — reached with Dio over the documented Postman collection. Four interceptors handle the bearer token, logging and error shaping; an expired token is detected from a real 401 rather than by decoding the token locally.

flow.title: Loading the home screen
steps: Three TMDB lists are requested independently over the http package.
Each call returns a sealed result — success or failure.
Each list has its own slot in the Home state, so they resolve separately.
Whichever lists arrived are rendered; a failed one shows its own message.
Opening a film pushes the details route over the root navigator, above the tab shell.

decisions: Use the http package rather than Dio: a read-only public API with a key needs no interceptors and no refresh.
Give each list its own slot in the state, so one failing request cannot blank the screen.
Return a sealed result from every call, so four developers working in parallel cannot forget a failure path.

challenges.title: One failing list blanking the whole screen
challenges.problem: Home shows three independent TMDB lists. Loading them into a single state meant one failing request left the screen empty even though the other two had data.
challenges.constraint: It had to stay one screen and one Cubit, not three nested ones.
challenges.approach: Give each list its own slot in the Home state so they resolve independently, and render whichever have arrived.
challenges.implementation: The Home Cubit holds three separate result slots rather than one combined list.
challenges.outcome: A failing list no longer empties the home screen; the other two still render.

challenges.title: Errors that were easy to forget
challenges.problem: Every call could fail, and nothing forced a developer to handle it — a missed failure path showed an empty list with no explanation.
challenges.constraint: Four developers were working in parallel, so the rule had to be enforced by the compiler, not by review.
challenges.approach: Return a sealed result type from every call and match on it with Dart 3 patterns, so a forgotten case fails the build.
challenges.implementation: A sealed ApiResult adopted across the team's repositories and use cases.
challenges.outcome: A forgotten error case is a compile error rather than a blank list at runtime.

challenges.title: Tabs that keep their place
challenges.problem: Opening a film from a tab and coming back should return to where the user was, and the details screen should not sit inside the bottom navigation.
challenges.constraint: Back navigation had to behave the same on both platforms.
challenges.approach: Use a go_router shell route for the tabs and push details over the root navigator, so the shell state survives and details covers the bar.
challenges.implementation: The shell route plus a root-level details route in the app router.
challenges.outcome: Tab state survives opening and closing a film.

items.name: Hen Lehen — API and backend

status.text: Backend built · not yet wired to the apps

items.summary: The server side I designed and built for the Hen Lehen platform: a FastAPI service over PostgreSQL and Redis, covering nineteen areas from appointments and payments to WebSocket chat and an audit log.
highlights: Nineteen endpoint modules and sixteen data models: patients, doctors, appointments, branches, chat, community, favourites, payments, reviews, specialties, medical records, notifications, devices, uploads and an admin dashboard.
Asynchronous throughout — async SQLAlchemy over asyncpg, Redis caching, Alembic migrations, JWT with hashed passwords, rate limiting, and real-time chat through a WebSocket manager.
Seventy-three tests covering chat, payments, security and database rules, and the WebSocket layer. I ran them: all seventy-three pass.
items.backend: This is the backend. FastAPI on Python with async SQLAlchemy over PostgreSQL, Redis for caching and rate-limit state, and Alembic migrations. Authentication is JWT issued with python-jose and passwords hashed with passlib/bcrypt; slowapi applies rate limiting, and a WebSocket endpoint carries the consultation chat. Nineteen endpoint modules cover auth, patients, doctors, specialties, appointments, medical records, payments, chat, community, reviews, favourites, branches, notifications, devices, uploads and admin.

items.note: It is not connected to the patient or doctor app yet, and I am not presenting those as backend-integrated. Wiring them is the next step, not a claim.

architecture.intro: FastAPI with async SQLAlchemy over PostgreSQL. Routers are thin: they validate with Pydantic and delegate to a service layer, so the rules live in one place and can be tested without an HTTP client. Schema changes go through Alembic rather than being applied by hand, so the database is reproducible from the repository.

flow.title: Booking an appointment, server side
steps: The appointment router receives the call and validates it with a Pydantic schema.
A JWT dependency resolves the caller; an unauthenticated request never reaches the rules.
The appointment service applies the rules — availability, ownership, state transitions.
Async SQLAlchemy writes through a session injected as a dependency.
A typed response schema goes back; rate limiting guards the public surface.

decisions: Keep routers thin and put the rules in a service layer, so they can be tested without an HTTP client.
Put every schema change in an Alembic migration, so the database is reproducible from the repository.
Use a WebSocket for consultation chat rather than a polling route, because polling is wasteful on a mobile connection.
Hash passwords and rate-limit the public surface from the start, rather than adding both later.

challenges.title: Two different clients, one set of rules
challenges.problem: Patients and doctors see the same appointments from opposite sides, and the rules about who may read or change what cannot live in either app.
challenges.constraint: Neither client can be trusted to enforce authorisation.
challenges.approach: Keep every rule in the service layer behind authenticated endpoints, so both applications get the same answer and neither decides what it is allowed to see.
challenges.implementation: Service modules separate from routers, with JWT-authenticated dependencies on the appointment, record and payment endpoints.
challenges.outcome: Both applications get the same authorisation answer, because neither decides what it may see.

challenges.title: A chat that cannot be polling
challenges.problem: A consultation needs messages to arrive as they are sent; polling would be both slow and wasteful on a mobile connection.
challenges.constraint: It had to sit inside the same authentication model as the REST surface.
challenges.approach: Add a WebSocket endpoint for the consultation room rather than a polling route.
challenges.implementation: A chat endpoint module carrying the socket connection, alongside the REST routers.
challenges.outcome: The whole stack comes up from a Compose file on a clean machine.

challenges.title: A database that can be rebuilt
challenges.problem: Schema changes applied by hand make an environment that only works on the machine it was built on.
challenges.constraint: The stack had to come up from scratch for anyone cloning the repository.
challenges.approach: Put every schema change in a migration and ship a Compose file that brings up PostgreSQL, Redis and the API together.
challenges.implementation: Alembic migrations plus docker-compose.yml and a Dockerfile in the backend directory.
challenges.outcome: 73 tests cover the endpoints and the service rules, and all pass.

quality.summary: 73 pytest functions across 7 files, covering the endpoints and the service rules. The suite was run during the audit and all 73 passed. Configuration is read from the environment rather than committed.
items: 73 pytest functions, all passing when run
Service layer testable without an HTTP client
Alembic migrations, so the schema is reproducible
Rate limiting and hashed passwords on the public surface

limits: The Flutter applications do not call this API yet — the client and repository exist on their integration branches, but the request is still commented out.

architecture.label: Architecture
architecture.title: How a request travels
architecture.intro: The same question for every app I build: where does state live, who is allowed to talk to the network, and what happens when the answer is an error. Pick a project to follow one request through its real layers.
architecture.note: Each path is read from that repository, including the one that does not reach a server yet.

layers: Widget
A screen renders state and dispatches events — no data access of its own.
BLoC / Cubit
One view-model per feature over an immutable freezed state.
Use case
One operation each, testable without Flutter.
Repository
An interface owned by the feature; the implementation chooses the data source.
Retrofit client
One per feature. Twenty-five typed routes across six services.
API gateway
Identity, catalog, address-cart, orders and payments behind one gateway, with Stripe and FCM alongside.
flows.fail: A 401 is handled in one place. The interceptor asks the refresh coordinator, which serialises concurrent callers onto a single refresh and replays the waiting requests with the new token — so an expired session does not become five competing refreshes and a forced logout. Routing calls use a separately named Dio instance, so a failure from the open routing service can never be mistaken for an authentication failure.

layers: Widget
The driver screen sends an event and renders whatever state comes back.
Bloc
One bloc per feature: application, sign-in, location.
Use case
Thin, so the rule being tested is the only thing in the test.
Repository
Split by concern — identity and orders are different clients, not one god service.
Retrofit clients
Nine endpoints, including the driver application as a multipart upload with licence and ID images.
REST backend
Base URL read from an environment file, never committed. Route geometry comes from OSRM, a third-party service.
flows.fail: A 401 does not reach the screen. An interceptor refreshes the bearer token, replays the original request once, and only surfaces an error if the retry also fails — so a driver mid-delivery is not thrown back to the login screen.

layers: Widget
Student and parent apps are separate, but both render from the same shared UI package.
Bloc
Per feature, with bloc_presentation for one-off effects and bloc_concurrency on the parent side.
Repository package
Each domain is its own package with two implementations behind one interface: Dio and a mock.
Shared HTTP client
One client for both apps. Interceptors attach the token, device id and locale.
EduCore API
Twenty domains for the student app, fifteen for the parent app, against one REST service.
flows.fail: An expired token is refreshed inside the interceptor before the call is replayed, so neither app has to know the session ended. Because every repository has a mock twin behind the same interface, a feature can be finished and tested before its endpoint exists.

layers: Widget
The exam screen owns no timing logic — it renders the session state.
Cubit
A timed exam engine that auto-submits on timeout and asks before the student leaves.
Use case
Start, answer, submit, review — one each.
Repository
Interfaces in the domain layer, Dio implementations behind them.
Dio + interceptors
Four: bearer token, logging, error shaping, and session expiry.
Elevate API
Their service, provided with the brief. Eleven routes wired against the documented collection.
flows.fail: Expiry is detected from a real 401 rather than by decoding the token on the device, so the client and the server never disagree about whether a session is alive. Several failing requests at once log the student out exactly once, not once per request.

layers: Widget
Arabic-first: the layout is wrapped in Directionality and driven by a locale provider written by hand.
ChangeNotifier
Provider holds session, booking and locale state across 23 screens.
Repository
AuthRepository exists on the integration branch, with the Dio client injected.
ApiClient
Configured with the base URL and a request interceptor — but the call inside the repository is still commented out.
In-memory data
So this is where the request stops today. The screens read a mock data set.
FastAPI backend
Built, migrated and tested — 19 endpoint modules, 16 models, 73 passing tests — and waiting to be called.
flows.fail: The honest state of this one: the backend is real and the client is in place, but no request is sent yet. Connecting them is the next piece of work, and this section says so rather than drawing a call that does not happen.
